body:
Origins of the Ahmadiyya Movement

The Ahmadiyya Movement emerged in Punjab during the late nineteenth century.

Its founder was Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (1835–1908), who lived at Qadian, a town in the Punjab region of British India, now in the Indian state of Punjab.

The movement was formally established in 1889. Its earliest organized following developed around the founder's religious teachings and claims.

The first formal initiation of followers took place in Ludhiana in 1889, while Qadian remained the principal geographical centre associated with the movement's origin.

Therefore, Qadian is the place most closely associated with the founder and the movement, while Ludhiana is important in accounts of its first formal initiation.

Religious Teaching and Claims

Mirza Ghulam Ahmad presented his movement as a renewal of religious life based on his interpretation of Islamic teachings.

He claimed to be the Promised Messiah and Mahdi. These were religious claims about an anticipated figure of spiritual guidance and renewal.

His claims became a major source of theological controversy. Many other Muslim religious scholars and communities rejected them, particularly because of differences concerning prophethood and religious authority.

The description of Mirza Ghulam Ahmad as the Promised Messiah and Mahdi refers to his own religious claim. It is not an uncontested belief shared by all Muslim traditions.

The Ahmadiyya Movement therefore developed a distinct theological identity. Its religious doctrines should not be treated as identical to those of the Aligarh or Deoband movements.

Religious Debate and Missionary Engagement

Religious controversy formed an important part of the movement's development.

Mirza Ghulam Ahmad engaged in written and oral debates with Christian missionaries, Hindu scholars and Muslim religious opponents.

The movement used printing, publication and public argument to explain and defend its teachings.

Its followers subsequently developed missionary activities beyond India. Translation of religious literature and organized preaching contributed to the movement's international reach.

These activities distinguish the movement from Aligarh's principal focus on modern educational institutions and Deoband's emphasis on traditional Islamic scholarship.

Relationship with Colonial Politics

The Ahmadiyya Movement emerged under British colonial rule, but its principal historical identity arose from religious teaching, controversy and missionary activity.

Mirza Ghulam Ahmad argued for a peaceful approach to religious propagation rather than armed religious struggle against the colonial government.

This position should be distinguished from the anti-colonial activities undertaken by some other Muslim religious movements.

It is also important not to treat all later Ahmadiyya followers and organizations as possessing an identical political position across different periods and countries.

Ahmadiyya and the Other Major Muslim Reform Movements

The most useful comparison concerns the problem each movement placed at the centre of its programme.

  • Aligarh: How can Muslims acquire modern education and advance under changing political and economic conditions?
  • Deoband: How can Islamic religious learning and practice be preserved and transmitted through organized education?
  • Ahmadiyya: How should religious renewal be understood through Mirza Ghulam Ahmad's claims, and how should those teachings be propagated?

All 3 movements used organized communication and educational or religious activity, but their central institutions, doctrines and historical programmes differed.

Prelims focus

  • Founder: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (1835–1908).
  • Foundation year: 1889.
  • Principal centre: Qadian, Punjab.
  • First formal initiation: Ludhiana, 1889.
  • Principal religious claims: Promised Messiah and Mahdi.
  • Historical activities: Religious debate, preaching, publication and missionary work.
  • Trap: The Ahmadiyya Movement was not founded by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, and it is distinct from the Deoband seminary.

[Sources: Oxford Academic, The Ahmadiyya Reform Movement, Oxford Handbook chapter abstract, 2026, sections on foundation, religious controversy and missionary expansion; Ahmadiyya Muslim Community, Tareekh-e-Ahmadiyyat, Qadian, the Partition of British India, and a Story of Sacrifice, introductory historical account; Ahmadiyya Muslim Jamaat Nigeria, Khilafat, section The First Person to Take Bai'at, 23 March 1889. Websites consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: The Ahmadiyya Movement: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, Religious Claims and Missionary Activity

body:
The Diversity of Muslim Reform

Aligarh, Deoband and Ahmadiyya were important movements, but they were not the only Muslim reform currents of colonial India.

Other movements developed around religious obligations, the authority of Islamic texts, customary practices, education and the social conditions of rural communities.

Their differences are especially important because similar names and overlapping religious terminology can lead to incorrect historical identification.

The Faraizi Movement

The Faraizi Movement arose in Bengal during the early nineteenth century.

Its founder was Haji Shariatullah (1781–1840), who had studied in Mecca and subsequently preached religious reform in Bengal.

The name Faraizi comes from faraiz, referring to obligatory religious duties in Islam.

Shariatullah called upon Muslims to observe their religious obligations and abandon customs that he considered inconsistent with Islamic teaching.

The movement became particularly influential among sections of the Muslim peasantry in eastern Bengal.

Dudu Miyan and Agrarian Grievances

After Shariatullah's death in 1840, his son Dudu Miyan, also known as Muhsinuddin Ahmad, became an important leader of the movement.

Under Dudu Miyan, the movement became more closely connected with agrarian grievances, including opposition to oppressive demands by landlords and the problems faced by cultivators.

The Faraizi Movement therefore illustrates how religious reform could develop a social and agrarian dimension.

Haji Shariatullah is associated with the religious foundation of the Faraizi Movement. Dudu Miyan is particularly associated with its later agrarian mobilization.

Tariqah-i-Muhammadiya and Sayyid Ahmad of Rae Bareli

Another important revivalist current was the Tariqah-i-Muhammadiya, associated with Sayyid Ahmad of Rae Bareli (1786–1831).

His movement emphasized religious reform, the unity of God and opposition to practices that its leaders considered unauthorized religious innovations.

It also developed a political and military dimension in northwestern India.

Sayyid Ahmad was killed in 1831 at Balakot while fighting Sikh forces.

Colonial accounts frequently applied the label Wahhabi to this and other revivalist networks. However, the Indian Tariqah-i-Muhammadiya movement had its own historical background and religious influences. It should not simply be identified as an exact extension of Arabian Wahhabism.

The Barelvi School of Thought

The Barelvi school developed in northern India during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

It is principally associated with Ahmad Raza Khan of Bareilly (1856–1921).

The movement developed within Sunni Islamic scholarship and emphasized particular understandings of devotion to Prophet Muhammad and the legitimacy of established devotional traditions.

Its teachings became influential in discussions concerning religious authority, customary devotional practices and relations between different schools of Islamic thought.

The Barelvi and Deoband traditions disagreed on important theological and devotional questions. However, both developed within broader Sunni Islamic traditions, and both had connections with forms of Sufi thought and practice. They should not be described simply as one movement supporting all Sufism and the other rejecting all Sufism.

Two Different Historical Figures with Similar Names

A particularly important distinction concerns Sayyid Ahmad of Rae Bareli and Ahmad Raza Khan of Bareilly.

They were different individuals associated with different movements and historical periods.

  • Sayyid Ahmad of Rae Bareli (1786–1831): Associated with the Tariqah-i-Muhammadiya revivalist movement and the conflict ending at Balakot in 1831.
  • Ahmad Raza Khan of Bareilly (1856–1921): Associated with the later Barelvi school of Sunni religious thought.

The Ahl-i-Hadith Current

The Ahl-i-Hadith current developed in nineteenth-century South Asia and emphasized direct engagement with the Quran and Hadith.

Its scholars questioned the necessity of following the interpretations of a single established school of Islamic jurisprudence in every matter.

It formed part of wider debates concerning religious authority, interpretation and the relationship between scripture and inherited scholarly practices.

It should be distinguished from Deoband, whose religious scholarship developed principally within the Hanafi legal tradition.

Nadwatul Ulama and Educational Reform

Nadwatul Ulama represented another approach to Muslim educational reform.

The movement is closely associated with Maulana Muhammad Ali Mungeri.

Its first major public meeting took place at Kanpur in 1894.

The institution known as Darul Uloom Nadwatul Ulama was established at Lucknow in 1898.

Its objective was to improve religious education through a curriculum that maintained Islamic scholarship while responding to contemporary educational needs, including greater attention to Arabic language and awareness of modern knowledge.

Nadwatul Ulama therefore illustrates an attempt to improve the curriculum of traditional religious institutions without simply adopting the Aligarh educational model.

How These Movements Differed

MovementPrincipal figureRegionHistorical emphasis
FaraiziHaji ShariatullahBengalReligious duties; later agrarian mobilization
Tariqah-i-MuhammadiyaSayyid Ahmad of Rae BareliNorth India and northwest frontierReligious revival and political-military activity
BarelviAhmad Raza KhanBareillySunni theology and devotional traditions
Ahl-i-HadithSeveral scholarsSouth AsiaAuthority of Quran and Hadith
Nadwatul UlamaMuhammad Ali MungeriKanpur and LucknowReform of religious educational curriculum

The table identifies each movement's central association. None of these movements can be fully explained through one activity alone, and their histories include internal differences and changes over time.

Prelims focus

  • Faraizi: Haji Shariatullah; Bengal; obligatory Islamic duties.
  • Dudu Miyan: Later Faraizi leader associated with agrarian grievances.
  • Sayyid Ahmad of Rae Bareli: Tariqah-i-Muhammadiya; died at Balakot in 1831.
  • Ahmad Raza Khan: Barelvi school of thought.
  • Nadwatul Ulama: First major public meeting at Kanpur in 1894; Lucknow seminary established in 1898.
  • Ahl-i-Hadith: Emphasis on Quran and Hadith as sources of religious authority.
  • Trap: Sayyid Ahmad of Rae Bareli, Ahmad Raza Khan of Bareilly and Sir Syed Ahmad Khan of Aligarh were 3 different historical figures.

[Sources: Banglapedia, Muslim Religious Movements, sections Faraizi, Tariqah-i-Muhammadiyah and Ahl-i-Hadith; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Barelvi, Sayyed Ahmad Shahid, sections on reformist ideas and the Balakot campaign; Oxford Academic, The Barelvi School of Thought, Oxford reference article, introduction, 2022; Darul Uloom Nadwatul Ulama, Nadwatul Ulama, institutional history, and Introduction to Darul Uloom. Websites consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Other Muslim Reform Currents: Faraizi, Tariqah-i-Muhammadiya, Barelvi and Nadwatul Ulama

body:
Understanding the Different Reform Approaches

The religious reform movements of nineteenth-century India emerged in response to changing social, political and intellectual circumstances. However, their founders did not all define reform in the same way.

The Ramakrishna–Vivekananda tradition placed major emphasis on spiritual harmony, Vedantic ideas, service to humanity and the moral regeneration of society.

The Aligarh Movement focused on modern education and community advancement under colonial rule.

The Deoband Movement concentrated on Islamic religious scholarship and the preservation of religious educational institutions.

The Ahmadiyya Movement developed around the distinct religious teachings and claims of Mirza Ghulam Ahmad and became associated with organized missionary activity.

Other Muslim reform currents emphasized religious obligations, devotional interpretation, reform of educational curricula or the grievances of rural communities.

Major Movements at a Glance

MovementLeading personalityPrincipal institution or placeCentral emphasis
Ramakrishna traditionSri RamakrishnaDakshineswar, BengalSpiritual experience and religious harmony
Neo-VedantaSwami VivekanandaChicago and Ramakrishna OrderPractical Vedanta, service and global engagement
Ramakrishna MissionSwami VivekanandaBelur Math, HowrahSpiritual life and organized humanitarian service
AligarhSir Syed Ahmad KhanMAO College, AligarhModern education and social advancement
DeobandMuhammad Qasim NanautaviDarul Uloom DeobandIslamic religious education and scholarship
AhmadiyyaMirza Ghulam AhmadQadian, PunjabDistinct religious claims and missionary activity
FaraiziHaji ShariatullahBengalReligious duties and later agrarian mobilization
Tariqah-i-MuhammadiyaSayyid Ahmad of Rae BareliNorth India and northwest frontierRevivalist teaching and political-military activity
BarelviAhmad Raza KhanBareillySunni theology and devotional tradition
Nadwatul UlamaMuhammad Ali MungeriKanpur and LucknowReform of religious education

Chronological Understanding

The chronology of the movements helps distinguish early religious revival, later educational reform and the growth of organized service institutions.

  • Early nineteenth century: The Faraizi and Tariqah-i-Muhammadiya movements developed in different regions.
  • 1831: Sayyid Ahmad of Rae Bareli died at Balakot.
  • 1864: Sir Syed's Scientific Society began its educational work.
  • 1866: Establishment of Darul Uloom Deoband according to institutional histories.
  • 1875: Aligarh school established.
  • 1877: Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College formally established.
  • 1889: Ahmadiyya Movement established.
  • 1893: Vivekananda addressed the World's Parliament of Religions at Chicago.
  • 1894: First major public meeting of Nadwatul Ulama.
  • 1897: Ramakrishna Mission founded.
  • 1898: Darul Uloom Nadwatul Ulama established at Lucknow; land acquired for the Belur monastery.
  • 1919: Jamiat Ulama-i-Hind established.
  • 1920: Aligarh Muslim University established from the earlier MAO College.

Distinguishing Theology from Educational and Political Activity

A movement's religious ideas, institutional priorities and political outlook must be distinguished. One does not automatically determine the others.

For example, the Aligarh Movement encouraged modern education and supported political caution under Sir Syed. Deoband emphasized religious scholarship, while several scholars associated with its tradition subsequently participated in anti-colonial politics.

Similarly, Vivekananda's ideas strengthened cultural self-confidence and influenced Indian national awakening, but the Ramakrishna Mission itself developed as a non-political spiritual and service organization.

The Ahmadiyya Movement's distinguishing historical features were its founder's religious claims and organized religious propagation, rather than the establishment of an Aligarh-type institution.

Important Distinctions in Historical Identification

Aligarh and Deoband Were Both Educational Movements

Both movements established influential educational institutions. The distinction lies in the subjects emphasized and the purposes for which education was promoted.

Aligarh emphasized Western sciences, English and preparation for participation in modern professional life. Deoband concentrated on Islamic religious education and the continuity of religious scholarship.

Religious Revival Was Not Necessarily Opposition to Modern Institutions

Religious reformers used printing, educational organization and public debate even when they disagreed about Western intellectual influences.

The use of modern communication methods did not necessarily mean acceptance of Western theological or social ideas.

Nationalism Took Different Forms

Religious and social reform influenced political consciousness in several ways.

Vivekananda encouraged cultural self-confidence and social uplift. Some Deobandi-associated scholars participated directly in anti-colonial movements. Sir Syed placed greater initial emphasis on education and cooperation with British authorities.

These positions belonged to particular leaders and historical circumstances. They should not be generalized to all followers across every period.

Similar Names Do Not Indicate the Same Founder

Sir Syed Ahmad Khan is associated with Aligarh. Sayyid Ahmad of Rae Bareli is associated with Tariqah-i-Muhammadiya. Ahmad Raza Khan of Bareilly is associated with the Barelvi school. Mirza Ghulam Ahmad founded the Ahmadiyya Movement.

Identifying the complete name together with the institution, region and period is more reliable than matching on one common word.

Prelims focus

  • Ramakrishna: Spiritual harmony; Vivekananda was his disciple.
  • Vivekananda: Chicago, 1893; Ramakrishna Mission, 1897.
  • Aligarh: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan; school, 1875; college, 1877; university, 1920.
  • Deoband: Muhammad Qasim Nanautavi; Islamic scholarship; founded in 1866 according to institutional histories.
  • Ahmadiyya: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad; Qadian; 1889.
  • Faraizi: Haji Shariatullah; Dudu Miyan and agrarian mobilization.
  • Trap: A movement's influence on nationalism, its religious beliefs and its educational priorities are separate historical characteristics and must not be assumed to be identical.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 8, printed pp. 106–107; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Print Culture and the Modern World, section 7, printed pp. 169–170; Belur Math, Swami Vivekananda and About Us; Aligarh Muslim University, History; Darul Uloom Waqf Deoband, institutional history; Oxford Academic, The Ahmadiyya Reform Movement, 2026; Banglapedia, Muslim Religious Movements; Oxford Academic, The Barelvi School of Thought, 2022; Darul Uloom Nadwatul Ulama, institutional history. Websites consulted 20 November 2026.]
